newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Singapore questions future of United Nations.
newsitem.headline: Singapore questions future of United Nations.

text.p: Singapore said on Thursday that the United Nations had less influence now than during the Cold War, with major powers turning the Security Council into a political theatre to soothe domestic concerns.

Yet Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar, in a hard-hitting speech to the U.N. General Assembly, said that nations big and small wasted hours on U.N. reforms in debates that "served to conceal and not clarify basic issues."
Efficiency, the need to spend less money, were proper concerns but did not deal with the key question of "efficiency to do what?"
"The sad truth is that today the United Nations plays little or no practical role in the management of the most important political, strategic and economic questions of our times," he said.
On Bosnia, he said the Security Council conducted a "political theatre to assauge the domestic concerns of some of its principle members."
And on economic issues, he said the U.N. "Agenda for Development," was mired in theological arguments on issues that were not so complicated.

"What the least developed most urgently need is not intellectual sophistry but help to build the institutions and formulate the policies that will allow them to plug into the global economy," Jayakumarhe said.
At a time when national decisions cannot be made in isolation, states are choosing other multinational forums outside of the United Nations.

Yet, he said, the big Second World War powers were hanging on to their domination of the U.N. Security Council. Any expansion of the council, under discussion for two years, would probably not extend the veto power to developing states.
"It is expecially difficult to imagine major powers allowing developing countries the veto over their policies."
At minimum, he said members should allow allow small states to join their closed-door consultations when issues concerned them.

"All the most important decisions of the Security Council are today made informally by the permanent members" -- the United States, Britain, China, Russia and France, with participation of other states merely symbolic.
"Formal session are clearly only a choreographed ritual to set the final seal of approval," he said.

On finances, he said that arguments made by some states, presumably Washington and to a lesser extent Moscow, about reducing their financial burdens, did not apply when they were called on to share power.

"There has never been any suggestion by any of the big powers that their control over critical U.N. expenditure decisions, in particular peacekeeping expenditures, should be proportionately diffused among the majority of small countries who are expected to take up the financial slack that they want to discard," he said.
